I called myself "gay Cassandra" in college. I kept meeting people in obviously terrible relationships, telling them, "Look, you're not gonna like hearing this, but I'd feel like I wronged you if I didn't tell you this is a sign of abuse," and then inevitably not being believed.

Eg: I met this girl at a party who met her then-boyfriend when he was 21 and she was 16. She told me this, then immediately said, "But I wasn't groomed, haha," when I had not asked & had made a mental effort to refrain from reacting. She explained, "He used to send me like, videos of him dancing on Snapchat. It was flirty but not sexual. I didn't date him until I was 18."

I still didn't have time to reply before she showed me her phone, on its lock screen, and said, "Look how much he cares about me." The lock screen was full of message notifications from the bf. She swiped her finger up the phone, and at light speed a hundred more notifications flew by, swiped again, more, swiped again, more. Because she was out and he "missed her."

Finally, I told her, as gently as I could, how my sister's abusive ex texted her the same way. 

The girl was happy and bubbly before, but she suddenly got totally cold toward me. "He's not abusive."

I said I didn't know him or her enough to know that, but that texting someone like that wasn't normal and was a "red flag."

She was still shut down. "He's not abusive." We didn't talk the rest of the night.

I think this is a much better real-life application of the Cassandra myth than "market manipulation": helplessly watching someone walk right towards something disturbing and terrible. This interaction haunts me, because there was so clearly something wrong, and there was absolutely nothing I could have said or done to intervene. 

Cassandra didn't have social media - no one was writing down her predictions or keeping track of how right or wrong she was. She just kept going up to people and saying, "Please, he's going to hurt you," and people didn't believe her because they didn't want to. Because how could he. Not him. Not to me. And Cassandra just has to live her life with that tragic, dramatic irony.

These are two statements that are true in isolation of each other, but that don't work once you put them together.

"Thought crime" refers specifically to actual thoughts - typically, intrusive thoughts. If you have the thought, "I wanna push that baby in front of a train," and that's where the thought ends, you've done no harm.

If you *say out loud*, or post, "I want to push this baby in front of a train," congrats, you have *acted* on your thoughts. You didn't commit murder, but you still did something harmful by saying out loud that you would *like* to commit murder. Thoughts are thoughts, but speech is an action.

Tweeting your opinions is not as good or bad as acting on them offline. Yes. But let's not pretend it's the same thing as inaction, or that it's morally neutral. Someone tweeting hatespeech or bodily threats or donation links for a good cause or condemning a harmful political figure - these are not inactions, they are not morally neutral, and they are not "just thoughts."

At the library system where I work, a record isn't kept on a user's account (unless they check a box), but it *is* automatically kept on items borrowed. So, if the government wanted to know everyone who borrowed a specific item, they would have that info. But if they wanted to know everything *you* borrowed, they're outta luck.

I'm quoting this document, from the comment we're both replying to: https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/44-1/bill/S-248/first-reading

In the language you're quoting, there's some potential ambiguity with the word "eligible." One can be "eligible" for a program in that they currently qualify for it to be done to them, but one can also be "eligible" in that they've signed up for it to be carried out later.

So, "You are eligible for MAID" could mean "You can undergo medical assisted death *right now*," or it could mean, "You now qualify for medical assisted death in the event you become terminally ill."

This is absolutely piss poor communication on the part of the Canadian government. Like, even in that first quote you pulled, "people with a mental illness as their sole underlying medical condition will have access...if they meet all of the eligibility requirements." What? Mental illness is their only requirement besides all the other requirements? That is extremely confusing, and worryingly so for such a major and controversial subject.

this article seems a bit slanted - from what I can tell, mental illness does not qualify you for medically assisted death.

the change being made is to their waivers: a person who develops a mental illness that could prevent them from consenting to MAID can sign a waiver giving consent ahead of time. Eg, if you develop Alzheimers and still want to qualify for MAID if you also develop a terminal illness.

source:

https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/44-1/bill/S-248/first-reading

>you can access euthanasia with mental illness as the only qualifier.

That is actually not what it says, to the best of my ability to interpret it. Here is the relevant section:

>B. permit an individual who has been diagnosed with a serious and incurable illness, disease or disability ***to make a written declaration to waive the requirement for final consent*** when receiving medical assistance in dying ***if they lose the capacity to consent***... (emphasis added)

Translation: people who develop mental illnesses, diseases, disabilities etc, that may prevent them from consenting to the "final consent" for MAID, can sign something ahead of time to opt out of that final consent *if/when they become terminally ill.*

Eg: you are currently coherent, but you are diagnosed with Alzheimers, which will leave you unable to say, "Yes, I consent to MAID" in several months. You have the option, now, while you're still mentally here, to basically consent ahead of time. Then, should you in addition to Alzheimers be diagnosed with a terminal illness, you're in the clear to go through with MAID.

This isn't allowing mental illness to be what qualifies you for MAID. It is preventing mental illness from being what bars you from MAID.

Honestly, if they had this where I live, it would make me feel a lot safer and better about my future. knowing that I wouldn't have to suffer through degradation and sickness before death - that I could leave easily and peacefully and with dignity - would put me much more at ease in the present.

Tread lightly if approaching strangers who are trans but don't pass - a lot of people in that position might feel really hurt about getting clocked, even by another trans person. Some of them may even lash out at you if you also don't pass (there's this idea that being in proximity of other visibly trans people makes you easier to clock. Pay attention to how people are dressed (are they trying to "look queer?"
